items.title: Roger Kellaway interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 14, 1999
items.q: And it will be with Chuck Domanico and Emil Richards, again

ctx.x: I have to say that — I’m not sure I can put this into words — that piece of music has so many different things in it, so many different emotions and styles. Every time I listen to it it seems to take on another dimension. And I’m wondering if other people felt that and if that’s why this music caught on with a real corps of listeners.

I don’t know. That corps of listeners is still there. I’ll tell you how this happened. I was doing a lot of studio work at the time in the late 60s, and I worked a lot with Edgar Lustgarden. And I had Edgar come over to my house and we played through a few original pieces. My desire was to write, I wanted to play piano and cello music but I wanted to write it. And Edgar was completely okay with that idea and that gave birth to the cello quartet, which became a marriage of wood. That was the whole point of that.…

subject of twentieth century classical music, perhaps too much for the jazz people who like me, but he said, “By the way the Kronos I saw last night and the cellist isn’t with them.” I said, “What? What happened?” She’s on sabbatical. I called my manager immediately, I said, “Find Joan Jeanrenaud.” And she called back the next day and we started talking about this idea.
